blocked.name: Bruine beuk (Copper Beech group)
blocked.reason: Register entry itself covers a group of six trees planted at the cemetery entrance ('vier dikkere bomen aan de rechterkant en twee aan de linkerkant', four thicker on the right, two on the left), not one identifiable specimen. No source found distinguishes one individual tree from the group, so it fails the one-collectible-point rule (an avenue/group planting, not a single point to stand at). Would need a source naming one specific standout tree within the group to become publishable.

Leave blocked under hard rule 10 unless a source establishes public visibility (e.g. it stands close enough to the street to be seen, per the Kromme Steenweg entries' shared address).

blocked.verify_notes: Register (netherlands-lrmb, nr 1696333): pedunculate oak (zomereik), planted band 1850-1860, in the wooded part ('bos') of the Warande park at De Kluis 2, owner_category gemeente, visitable ja, visible nee (stands off the main path but reachable). Register's own history note: 'one of the few specimens still surviving from the layout of the Warande in the mid-nineteenth century, around 1850-1860.' Corroborated in general terms, not tree-specifically, by Dutch Wikipedia's Warande park article (oldest plantings still present date from 1834, most of the oldest trees from around 1850, monumental oaks named among them) and by the Monumentenwerkgroep Helmond's own Warande page, which independently notes many oaks in the park were felled and replanted between 1830 and 1860, and that a different oak that fell in a 2018 storm was aged at roughly 150 years (so grown from an acorn around 1865), consistent with the register's stated planting band for surviving oaks of the same generation. No girth on file. A second, similarly-dated register oak (nr 1696332, also 'Zomereik', planted band 1850-1860) stands about 400-500 m away elsewhere in the same park; not included here to avoid a near-duplicate entry, recorded as a lead.

blocked.verify_notes: Register (netherlands-lrmb, nr 1683271): London plane (gewone plataan), planted band 1830-1840, multi-stemmed ('meerstammig'), owner_category gemeente, visitable ja, visible ja. Register's own history note: the tree once stood beside the house of physician/manufacturer Holtus, on the banked shore of the Ameide (a branch of the Aa that rejoined it via the Koninginnewater); the associated house dates from around 1870 and the register text adds 'the tree is also roughly dateable [from that]', which is inconsistent with the register's own numeric planted_band of 1830-1840 (40 years earlier). Flagging this discrepancy rather than picking a winner: I am using the register's dated field (1830-1840) as the estimate since it is the structured data point, not the prose aside. A local news item (ditishelmond.nl, on a separate weeping willow behind the Stadskantoor) independently confirms mature registered/monumental trees stand on this same municipal plot and that the municipality treats them as worth preserving through redevelopment, but does not name this specific plane tree or give it an age; a municipality Q&A page about tree preservation during the 'Huis voor de Stad' redevelopment (helmond.nl) returned a server error (HTTP 500) on two attempts and could not be used. No girth on file.

Second source (online-begraafplaatsen.nl and general search results) independently confirms this cemetery, formerly the Sint Lambertus/R.K. burial ground, was established in 1880 as an expansion of an earlier, smaller Molenstraat cemetery, and that its grounds carry trees dating from that founding period onward, i.e. a wooded, historic cemetery layout consistent with a circa-1900s weeping beech, though the source does not name this individual tree. This is a public cemetery, not a private garden; grounds are open in daylight to visitors as with any Dutch municipal/parish cemetery. No girth on file.
